answer.summary: Dietrich’s advice is to build a product people love and naturally share, keep improving it consistently, and prepare the company and its leaders to scale quickly. Word of mouth matters, but it is not the only growth channel.

sections.heading: Build a product that creates natural growth
sections.content: Start with an amazing, differentiated product customers love using. Dietrich says hypergrowth requires organic, inbound, and viral word of mouth: users should encounter natural opportunities to bring others in—for example, inviting colleagues to collaborate on a Miro board or Confluence pages. She argues this kind of user-to-user selling is more efficient than relying only on salespeople, and that a company cannot simply pay enough to sustain hypergrowth while remaining viable.

sections.heading: Keep improving and use the growth channels that fit
sections.content: Hypergrowth is not a magic bullet. Dietrich emphasizes consistency, customer obsession, and incremental improvements across the business. She also says other channels matter: at Atlassian, SEO was the number-one marketing motion, and paid search contributed roughly 15–25% of leads at the time. So word of mouth is important, but not an exclusive route to growth.

sections.heading: Prepare the company for the next stage
sections.content: Companies in hypergrowth can move through stages that take others five or ten years, such as going from 10 to 50, 50 to 100, or 100 to 200. Dietrich recommends hiring 2X- and 3X-level leaders who have seen the next stage, while developing homegrown talent; hiring ahead, using advisors, and building relationships with mentors who know what good looks like at the next scale can help. Major growth levers also need to be funded, thoughtfully constructed, and treated as cross-company strategy—not left to one department. For example, moving upmarket requires coordinated marketing, product, research, support, and sales efforts.

answer.summary: Dietrich’s core recipe is a product people love, organic word of mouth and viral use, and leaders ready for the next growth stage. She also stresses consistent customer-focused improvement and treating growth as a funded, company-wide strategy. [S1, S2, S3, S6]

sections.heading: Build a product that creates its own pull
sections.content: Start with a differentiated, amazing product that customers love using. Aim for organic, inbound growth and viral word of mouth: Dietrich says companies cannot pay enough to sustain hypergrowth rates and remain viable. Miro illustrates the effect—people used its whiteboards to capture and iterate on ideas, then brought others in. [S1, S4]

sections.heading: Prepare the company for each leap in scale
sections.content: Hypergrowth companies can move through stages that take others five or ten years—for example, going from 10 to 50, 50 to 100, or 100 to 200. Keep hiring 2X- and 3X leaders who have seen the next stage; homegrown talent can grow too, but leaders should seek mentors, advisors, and peers who know what operating at the next scale requires. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: Make growth sustained and company-wide
sections.content: Do not expect a magic bullet: keep listening to customers and make consistent, incremental improvements across the business. Treat major growth levers—such as product-led versus sales-assisted growth, new products or segments, verticals, global expansion, and partner channels—as funded, thoughtfully constructed company strategies, not isolated departmental goals. Align product, marketing, research, support, and sales around the chosen direction. [S3, S6, S5]

sections.heading: Use channels that fit; do not rely on virality alone
sections.content: Dietrich says other channels matter too. At Atlassian, SEO was the number-one marketing motion, and paid search accounted for roughly 15–25% of leads at the time. [S7, S3]
